tier_reason: First-party benchmark (the author's own docs site, code in benchmarks/http1.py) against httptools 0.8.0, which wraps llhttp. The page gives no CPU model (only "an Apple Silicon machine") and no Zig compiler version, so it is not A. It is not an independent suite or a paper, so it is not B either: first-party code with partial methodology is C.

corrections.baseline: llhttp (via MagicStack/httptools 0.8.0, the Python binding over llhttp)
corrections.claimed_speedup: beats httptools on 13 of 14 workloads, 1.04x-2.06x faster (e.g. 1.16x on wrk default GET, 2.42M vs 2.09M msg/s; 2.06x on 16KB upload in MTU pieces, 441k vs 214k msg/s; 1.18x on 'Chunked POST (llhttp bench)', 875k vs 741k msg/s; 1.14x on 'Real-world GET (pico/llhttp)', 947k vs 831k msg/s); 0.94x (slower) on the synthetic TFB plaintext 16x-pipelined workload, 151k vs 161k msg/s
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Zig ReleaseSafe build (safety checks on); the page gives no Zig version (the repo's pyproject.toml pins ziglang==0.16.0 as a build requirement); CPython 3.14; httptools 0.8.0
corrections.caveats: Only a first-party benchmark. Hardware is described only as "an Apple Silicon machine", with no exact CPU model, and the page gives no Zig compiler version. The author puts run-to-run spread at about 5%, which is about the size of several of the smaller wins (1.04x-1.08x). The benchmark measures parser throughput in isolation through Python bindings on both sides, not a full server. The live docs page is stale: the repo's docs/reference/performance.md at HEAD (refreshed in commit 50248abe, 2026-08-27; CPython 3.14.3, zttp 0.0.27.dev38, median of 15 batches) reports zttp faster on all 14 workloads, 1.01x-2.55x (pipelined 1.25x, MTU-pieces upload 2.55x), but the deployed site has not been rebuilt with those numbers.

notes: The live page's numbers match the record except for one mislabel: 1.14x is the Real-world GET (pico/llhttp) row, while the llhttp chunked-POST row is 1.18x (fixed in claimed_speedup). The tier was B, but this is first-party code with partial methodology, so it is C. The newer, stronger numbers in the repo docs are recorded in caveats, and enrichment may prefer them once they are deployed.

tier_reason: The only numbers are first-party cargo #[bench] output pasted into the README. The benchmark code (benches/parse.rs) is public and compares against picohttpparser via picohttpparser-sys, but no CPU model or rustc nightly version is given, so it is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README cargo bench output. With RUSTFLAGS="-C target-feature=+sse4.2": full request thhp 4421 MB/s (159 ns/iter +/- 23) vs picohttpparser 4393 MB/s (160 ns/iter +/- 37), about 1.006x (derived from page data), within the stated noise; short request thhp 1600 MB/s vs picohttpparser 1244 MB/s, about 1.29x (derived from page data). Without the flag: full request thhp 3550 MB/s vs picohttpparser 4594 MB/s, so thhp is slower (about 0.77x, derived from page data); short request thhp 1513 MB/s vs picohttpparser 1333 MB/s, about 1.14x (derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: cargo +nightly bench (nightly version unstated); Cargo.toml [profile.bench] sets opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1; the explicit run sets RUSTFLAGS="-C target-feature=+sse4.2" and the implicit run sets no RUSTFLAGS; the baseline picohttpparser-sys 1.0 is built with its "sse4" feature in both runs
corrections.stars_or_usage: 15 stars; about 5,000 all-time crates.io downloads (41 recent), latest version 0.2.0 (2018)
corrections.caveats: Numbers are first-party only, with no CPU model and no nightly rustc version stated. On the full, realistic request the win over picohttpparser is only there with explicit SSE4.2, and even then it is about 0.6%, inside the +/- noise shown. Without the flag thhp is about 23% slower on that request. The consistent win is on the short request (about 1.29x with explicit SSE4.2, about 1.14x without), and only there. The README makes no explicit 'faster than picohttpparser' claim beyond its 'Very Fast HTTP Parser' title and the bench output. Last commit was in 2018.

notes: The benchmark_url (benches/parse.rs) is the bench code and does compare against picohttpparser, but it has no numbers. They are in the README Benchmark section, so benchmark_url is corrected to that. The record left out that thhp still beats pico on the short request without explicit SSE4.2 (1513 vs 1333 MB/s), so it is faster on the short request in both configurations and not a 'not-faster' reject. Tier C is unchanged.

tier_reason: Upgraded from D. LiteSpeed's own 'Fast Huffman Encoder' post (2019-10-03) publishes median timings of ls-hpack's HPACK Huffman encoder against nghttp2's, nginx's and h2o's. The code is public in litespeedtech/benchmarks/huffman-encoder (comp-enc driver, bench.pl, Makefile CFLAGS -O3 -DNDEBUG -g0), but the post gives no CPU model and no compiler version, so it is first-party C, not A.

corrections.baseline: nghttp2 (HPACK); the numeric benchmark covers only nghttp2's HPACK Huffman encoder (nghttp2_hd_huffman.c at revision 0e1d0400d86a)
corrections.workload: HPACK Huffman string encoding microbenchmark (RFC 7541 Huffman code). Code extracted from each project into litespeedtech/benchmarks/huffman-encoder and run for a fixed iteration count on 4 inputs: 'LiteSpeed' (small), a real x-fb-debug header value from the Facebook response QIF (medium), the same value with backslashes to force the fallback path, and several paragraphs of prose (large). Median of 5 runs. The companion decoder benchmark compares only against nginx 1.16.1's Huffman decoder.
corrections.claimed_speedup: ls-hpack's fast Huffman encoder vs nghttp2's encoder, in seconds (median of 5): 'LiteSpeed' 8.67 vs 20.59 (2.37x), x-fb-debug 5.25 vs 30.31 (5.77x), x-fb-backslash 7.22 vs 32.21 (4.46x), idle text 9.32 vs 52.25 (5.61x). The same post also has it 1.11x-2.12x faster than nginx's encoder and 1.18x-3.59x faster than h2o's. The companion 'Fast Huffman Decoder' post (2019-09-16) reports 1.15x-1.96x faster than nginx 1.16.1's decoder, which it says derives from nghttp2's 4-bit decoder. Bun's build script separately says ls-hpack is "faster than nghttp2's for our workloads", with no numbers.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Makefile CFLAGS=-Wall -DNDEBUG -O3 -g0; compiler and version not stated
corrections.stars_or_usage: 56 stars; vendored by oven-sh/bun (scripts/build/deps/lshpack.ts) and a git submodule of litespeedtech/lsquic (1,876 stars); used in LiteSpeed Web Server
corrections.caveats: The only numbers are first-party (LiteSpeed blog, 2019) and cover the HPACK Huffman encoder component only, not full HPACK encode/decode against nghttp2's HPACK API. Each project's code was extracted into standalone C files, and the nghttp2 copy is a 2019 revision (0e1d0400d86a), so current nghttp2 may differ. No CPU model or compiler version is stated. The litespeedtech/benchmarks repo has no license file (the benchmark harness only; ls-hpack itself is MIT). The decoder benchmark compares only against nginx's decoder, not nghttp2's. Bun's adoption comment gives no numbers.

notes: benchmark_url was null. A brief search of LiteSpeed's blog and repos found real numbers against nghttp2 (the Huffman encoder post plus its public harness in litespeedtech/benchmarks), so benchmark_url is corrected and the tier goes from D to C. page_compares_against_baseline and numbers_found_on_page refer to that corrected URL. The record's 'metric: other' could reasonably become 'throughput' (time for a fixed iteration count), but metric is not a correctable field.
